title: New Dish on the Menu
story: A small café prints its menu with dishes listed from cheapest to most expensive. Prices are stored in cents, so 420 means 4.20. Two dishes can cost the same.

The cook has a new dish and a price for it. The printer needs to know which line the new dish goes on so the menu stays sorted. If other dishes already have that exact price, the new one is listed before them, so the newest dish gets seen first.
task: Write insertPosition(prices, price). prices is sorted from smallest to largest and may contain repeats. Return the index where price should be inserted: the first index whose price is greater than or equal to price. If every price is smaller, return prices.length.
Do not change the list. An empty menu returns 0. Aim for O(log n).
constraints: prices is sorted in non-decreasing order.

examples.explanation: 350, 420 and 420 are all cheaper than 500. The first price that is 500 or more is 575, at index 3, so the new dish goes there and pushes 575 down a line.
Two dishes already cost 420. The new one goes before both of them, at index 1. Index 3 (after them) would be a valid sorted spot too, but the café's rule says before.

hints: In [350, 420, 420, 575, 890], mark each price as "smaller than 500" or "not". What shape does that row of marks have?
It is always a block of "smaller" followed by a block of "not smaller", because the list is sorted. You want the first position of the second block.

Binary search for that boundary instead of for a value. If the middle price is smaller than price, the boundary is to its right. Otherwise the middle itself might be the boundary, so you cannot throw it away.
Start with lo = 0 and hi = n (one past the end, because the answer can be n). While lo < hi: if prices[mid] < price set lo = mid + 1, else hi = mid. When they meet, that is the answer.
bruteForce: Walk from the start and return the first index whose price is at least price, or n if you reach the end.

That is O(n): up to 100,000 checks for one dish. A plain binary search that stops as soon as it finds an equal price is faster but wrong here: in the second example its first look lands on index 2, one of the two 420s, and it returns 2 instead of 1.

most expensive of all: position equals the length
all the same price: goes first, not last

js: let lo = 0, hi = prices.length; // the answer is somewhere in [lo, hi]
if (prices[mid] < price) lo = mid + 1; // mid is too cheap: boundary is right of it
else hi = mid;                         // mid could be the boundary: keep it
py: lo, hi = 0, len(prices)  # the answer is somewhere in [lo, hi]
lo = mid + 1  # mid is too cheap: boundary is right of it
hi = mid  # mid could be the boundary: keep it
walkthrough: Instead of searching for a value, search for a boundary: the first price that is not smaller than the new one. Everything left of it is smaller, everything from it on is not.
• lo = 0, hi = 5, mid = 2. 420 is not smaller than 420, so index 2 might be the boundary. hi = 2.
• lo = 0, hi = 1, mid = 0. 350 < 420, so the boundary is to the right. lo = 1.

Two details make this work. First, hi starts at n, not n - 1, because "after everything" is a valid answer. Second, when the middle is big enough you set hi = mid, not mid - 1: the middle might be the answer itself. The loop still ends, because mid is always strictly less than hi.
solution.timeWhy: The range [lo, hi] halves every round.
solution.takeaway: Many searches are really "find the first position where a yes/no condition turns true". Start with hi = n, set hi = mid when the condition holds and lo = mid + 1 when it does not. This lower-bound loop is the same as bisect_left in Python.
